question: Did IBM's published calibration data predict the good vs bad window?
author: elder
method: backend.properties(datetime=...) historical snapshots at each job's execution time, qubits [53,54,55], ibm_marrakesh

k5_contrast_retention_predicted_from_pub.note: exp(-62*(e1+e2)) depolarizing model, 124 CZ split across two pairs

verdict: NO. Published calibration is essentially flat across the two windows (predicts a 3% k5-contrast difference; observed 3x, i.e. ~100x larger effect than predicted). Both windows are ALSO mispredicted in absolute terms in OPPOSITE directions: bad window much worse than its published numbers imply, good window much better (observed 0.99 vs predicted 0.81). The k0 systematic (-0.045) in the good window likewise exceeds published readout error (~0.005-0.01) by ~5x. Whatever drifted between windows is not captured by published RB gate errors, readout errors, or T1/T2.
implications: The 'free window picker from published calibration' shortcut is DEAD as-is: published numbers cannot qualify or disqualify a window (mirrors the FakeMarrakesh 400x miss, which is built from the same published data).
Same-session measured sentinel remains the ONLY validated window gate (F81 Rec#5 rule).
Weak residual hypothesis, untested: time-since-calibration (38min vs 79min) or unpublished coherent-error alignment; would need the window-distribution accumulation probes to test.
T1/T2 identical across snapshots = those fields were not re-measured between calibrations; they carry no window information at this cadence.
